result.markdown: --- title: "Session 1 — Know Your Data, Choose Your Test" subtitle: "Variable types · describing data · checking it · choosing a test · reading a result · Lab 1" author: "Community Medicine Workshop" format: revealjs: theme: serif css: [../assets/slide_deck.css, assets/workshop.css, assets/quiz.css] include-after-body: assets/quiz-include.html embed-resources: true slide-number: true navigation-mode: linear code-copy: true center: false transition: fade width: 1280 height: 720 fig-align: center html-math-method: plain execute: echo: true warning: false message: false fig-width: 9 fig-height: 4.6 fig-dpi: 100 --- ## Where we are ::: {.incremental} - The **Basic** track showed *which* test to run and *how* to run it in R - This workshop adds the two things a thesis examiner asks about: - **Were the assumptions met?** How did you check, and what did you do if not? - **What does the result mean?** In words, with an effect size and a confidence interval - By the end of today you can: - classify variables and describe them correctly - **check the data** before testing anything - choose a test from four questions - read a p-value, a confidence interval and an effect size ::: ## Our data ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="52%"} - **631 adults** screened for NCDs (`data/prac_modded.xlsx`, the practice dataset of the Basic track) - Sex, age, wealth index, marital status, poverty line - Screening history, past hypertension and diabetes - Blood pressure, glucose, height, weight - Foot pain **before and after** an intervention - Fasting glucose and SBP at **presentation, 3 and 6 months** ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> select(sex_of_participants, age_of_participants, wealth_index_of_participants, sbp_in_mm_hg) |> head(5) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 4 sex_of_participants age_of_participants wealth_index_of_partici…¹ sbp_in_mm_hg 1 male 26 middle 128 2 male 47 richest 107 3 female 44 richest 112 4 female 19 richest 126 5 female 60 richest 109 # ℹ abbreviated name: ¹​wealth_index_of_participants ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: # Topic 1 — What kind of variable? {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Four kinds of variable | Type | What it is | In our data | |---|---|---| | **Nominal** | categories, no order | sex, marital status, diabetes yes/no | | **Ordinal** | categories **with order**, gaps not equal | wealth index (poorest → richest) | | **Interval** | numbers, equal gaps, **no true zero** | temperature in °C (not in our data) | | **Ratio** | numbers, equal gaps, **true zero** | age, weight, SBP, glucose | ::: {.key} The **outcome's type** decides the family of tests: counts and percentages for categories; means or medians for numbers. ::: ## Describing a category: counts and percentages ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> count(wealth_index_of_participants) |> mutate(percent = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 5 × 3 wealth_index_of_participants n percent 1 poorest 34 5.4 2 poorer 106 16.8 3 middle 147 23.3 4 richer 177 28.1 5 richest 167 26.5 ``` ::: ::: - Give the **order** for ordinal variables (`factor(..., levels = ...)`), or R sorts them alphabetically - Always report **n and %**, and the denominator if anything is missing ## Describing a number: mean or median? {.smaller} ::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> summarise(mean = mean(age_of_participants), sd = sd(age_of_participants), median = median(age_of_participants), q1 = quantile(age_of_participants, .25), q3 = quantile(age_of_participants, .75)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 5 mean sd median q1 q3 1 43.8 17.4 42 29 58 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(p, aes(age_of_participants)) + geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = col_blue, colour = "white") + labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Adults") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](s1_know_your_data_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=550} ::: ::: ::: ::: **Symmetric** → mean (SD); **skewed** or outliers → median (IQR). Age is a little right-skewed: mean 43.8 > median 42. # Topic 2 — Check before you test {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## A test cannot rescue bad data ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p |> summarise(sbp_below_dbp = sum(sbp_in_mm_hg < dbp_in_mm_hg), median_dbp = median(dbp_in_mm_hg), min_sbp_follow_up = min(c(sbp_3_months, sbp_6_months)), max_sbp_follow_up = max(c(sbp_3_months, sbp_6_months))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 sbp_below_dbp median_dbp min_sbp_follow_up max_sbp_follow_up 1 104 108 38 387 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.warn} In 104 adults the systolic pressure is **lower** than the diastolic, the median DBP is 108 mmHg, and follow-up SBP runs from 38 to 387 mmHg. These are recording problems, not biology. ::: ## What to do with suspicious values ::: {.incremental} 1. **Look** at every variable first: `summary()`, a histogram, impossible combinations (SBP < DBP) 2. **Query** the source (case sheet, register) and correct what can be corrected 3. Decide **before** testing what you exclude, and **report it** ("12 records with SBP < DBP were excluded") 4. Run the analysis **with and without** the doubtful records: a **sensitivity analysis** ::: ::: {.key} In this workshop the blood pressure columns are used to practise tests on skewed, messy data. The cleaner variables (height, weight, fasting glucose, age) carry the parametric tests. ::: # Topic 3 — Choosing a test {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Four questions choose the test ::: {.incremental} 1. **What is the outcome?** Category (yes/no, groups) or number (mmHg, kg)? 2. **How many groups** am I comparing? One (against a known value), two, or more? 3. **Paired or independent?** Same people measured twice (before/after), or different people? 4. **Do the assumptions hold?** Roughly normal, similar spread, enough expected counts? ::: ::: {.key} Questions 1–3 come from the **study design** and are fixed before you see the data. Only question 4 is checked on the data (Session 2). ::: ## The map: category outcome | Comparison | Independent groups | Paired (same people) | |---|---|---| | One group vs expected proportions | **Chi-square goodness of fit** | — | | 2 × 2 table | **Chi-square**; **Fisher's exact** if an expected count < 5 | **McNemar** (exact McNemar if few discordant pairs) | | Larger table (r × c) | **Chi-square** if ≥ 80% of expected counts ≥ 5 and none < 1; else **Monte Carlo** or **Fisher** | — | | Several predictors at once | **Logistic regression** (Regression track) | — | ## The map: number outcome | Comparison | Roughly normal | Skewed, ordinal or outliers | |---|---|---| | One group vs a known value | **one-sample t** | **one-sample Wilcoxon** | | Two independent groups | **Welch t** | **Mann–Whitney U** | | Two paired measurements | **paired t** | **Wilcoxon signed-rank** | | ≥ 3 independent groups | **one-way ANOVA** (Welch ANOVA if spreads differ) | **Kruskal–Wallis** | | ≥ 3 repeated measurements | **repeated-measures ANOVA** | **Friedman** | | Two numbers together | **Pearson r** | **Spearman ρ** | # Topic 4 — Reading a result {background-color="#2C3E50"} ## Three numbers, not one ::: {.incremental} - **Effect size**: *how big* is the difference? (difference in means, odds ratio, Cohen's d, r) - **95% confidence interval**: the range of effect sizes compatible with the data - **p-value**: *if there were truly no difference*, how often would data at least this extreme turn up by chance? ::: ::: {.warn} A p-value is **not** the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says **nothing about size or importance**. p > 0.05 is **not** proof of no difference. ::: ## Example: weight in women and men ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t.test(weight ~ sex_of_participants, data = p) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: weight by sex_of_participants t = 0.61506, df = 607.63, p-value = 0.5387 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group female and group male is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: -1.655836 3.165961 sample estimates: mean in group female mean in group male 70.04272 69.28766 ``` ::: ::: ## The sentence to write ::: {.eq} "Mean weight was 70.0 kg in women and 69.3 kg in men (difference 0.8 kg, 95% CI -1.7 to 3.2; Welch t-test, p = 0.539; Cohen's d = 0.05)." ::: ::: {.incremental} - Women vs men: from **1.7 kg lighter to 3.2 kg heavier**. The data rule out a large difference - d = 0.05 is **negligible** (rough guide: 0.2 small, 0.5 medium, 0.8 large) - Say "no evidence of a difference", never "the groups are the same" ::: ## 🔧 Switch to R — Lab 1 {.lab-slide background-color="#1565c0"} ::: {.lab-box} **File:** `stats-workshop/labs/lab1_describe.R` - counts and percentages, with the wealth index in order - mean (SD) and median (IQR), and which to report - impossible and suspicious values, and how many - choosing the test for five research questions ::: **Time:** 30 minutes · answer the Q questions in the comments ## Self-check quiz (1/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t1q1" data-type="mcq" data-hash="8ufvjc.xu9umj" data-show="T3JkaW5hbCwgYmVjYXVzZSBpdHMgbGV2ZWxzIGhhdmUgYW4gb3JkZXIgYnV0IHVuZXF1YWwg Z2Fwcw==" data-explain="VGhlIGNhdGVnb3JpZXMgYXJlIG9yZGVyZWQgKHBvb3Jlc3QgdG8gcmljaGVzdCkgYnV0IHRo ZSBkaXN0YW5jZSBiZXR3ZWVuIHRoZW0gaXMgbm90IGEgbWVhc3VyZWQgcXVhbnRpdHksIHNv IHRoZSB2YXJpYWJsZSBpcyBvcmRpbmFsLg=="} The wealth index (poorest, poorer, middle, richer, richest) is which kind of variable? - Nominal, because its levels are labels with no order - Ordinal, because its levels have an order but unequal gaps - Interval, because each level is exactly one equal step apart - Ratio, because the poorest level is a true zero point ::: ## Self-check quiz (2/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t1q2" data-type="mcq" data-hash="8ug8s1.xua93w" data-show="TWVkaWFuIGFuZCBpbnRlcnF1YXJ0aWxlIHJhbmdlLCBiZWNhdXNlIGl0IGlzIHNrZXdlZA==" data-explain="U2tldyBhbmQgb3V0bGllcnMgcHVsbCB0aGUgbWVhbiBhbmQgaW5mbGF0ZSB0aGUgU0QuIFRo ZSBtZWRpYW4gYW5kIElRUiBkZXNjcmliZSB0aGUgdHlwaWNhbCB2YWx1ZSBhbmQgc3ByZWFk IHdpdGhvdXQgYmVpbmcgZHJhZ2dlZCBieSB0aGUgdGFpbC4="} Fasting glucose is strongly right-skewed with a few very high values. How should you summarise it? - Mean and standard deviation, because it is a number - Median and interquartile range, because it is skewed - Mode and range, because the high values are outliers - Mean and standard error, because the sample is large ::: ## Self-check quiz (3/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t1q3" data-type="mcq" data-hash="8ugm0r.xuanla" data-show="UXVlcnkgdGhlIHNvdXJjZSByZWNvcmRzLCB0aGVuIGRlY2lkZSBhbmQgcmVwb3J0IHdoYXQg dG8gZXhjbHVkZQ==" data-explain="SW1wb3NzaWJsZSB2YWx1ZXMgYXJlIHJlY29yZGluZyBwcm9ibGVtcy4gQ2hlY2sgdGhlIHNv dXJjZSwgY29ycmVjdCB3aGF0IHlvdSBjYW4sIGRlY2lkZSBvbiBleGNsdXNpb25zIGJlZm9y ZSB0ZXN0aW5nLCByZXBvcnQgdGhlbSwgYW5kIGNvbXBhcmUgcmVzdWx0cyB3aXRoIGFuZCB3 aXRob3V0IHRoZW0u"} You find 104 records where systolic pressure is lower than diastolic. What should you do first? - Run the planned test, because a large sample absorbs a few errors - Delete those rows quietly so the results look cleaner - Query the source records, then decide and report what to exclude - Swap the two columns for those rows and carry on testing ::: ## Self-check quiz (4/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t1q4" data-type="mcq" data-hash="8ugz9h.xub22o" data-show="TWNOZW1hciB0ZXN0LCBiZWNhdXNlIHRoZSBzYW1lIHBlb3BsZSB3ZXJlIG1lYXN1cmVkIHR3 aWNl" data-explain="QmVmb3JlIGFuZCBhZnRlciBpbiB0aGUgc2FtZSBwZW9wbGUgYXJlIHBhaXJlZC4gRm9yIGEg cGFpcmVkIHllcy9ubyBvdXRjb21lIHRoZSBNY05lbWFyIHRlc3QgdXNlcyB0aGUgcGVvcGxl IHdobyBjaGFuZ2VkICh5ZXMgdG8gbm8sIG5vIHRvIHllcyku"} Foot pain (yes/no) was recorded in the same adults before and after an intervention. Which test compares the two? - Chi-square test of independence on the before-after 2 x 2 table - Fisher's exact test, because the outcome has only two levels - Paired t-test on the yes/no answers coded as 0 and 1 - McNemar test, because the same people were measured twice ::: ## Self-check quiz (5/5) {.smaller} ::: {.quiz-q data-qid="t1q5" data-type="mcq" data-hash="8uhci3.xubgjy" data-show="Tm8gZXZpZGVuY2Ugb2YgYSBkaWZmZXJlbmNlOyBhIGxhcmdlIGRpZmZlcmVuY2UgaXMgdW5s aWtlbHk=" data-explain="QSBsYXJnZSBwLXZhbHVlIG1lYW5zIHRoZSBkYXRhIGFyZSBjb21wYXRpYmxlIHdpdGggbm8g ZGlmZmVyZW5jZTsgdGhlIENJIHNob3dzIHdoaWNoIGRpZmZlcmVuY2VzIHJlbWFpbiBwbGF1 c2libGUgKGhlcmUgc21hbGwgb25lcykuIEl0IGlzIG5ldmVyIHByb29mIG9mIGVxdWFsaXR5 LCBhbmQgdGhlIHAtdmFsdWUgaXMgbm90IHRoZSBwcm9iYWJpbGl0eSB0aGF0IEgwIGlzIHRy dWUu"} A comparison gives p = 0.54 with a 95% CI for the difference of -1.7 to 3.2 kg. What is the right reading? - No evidence of a difference; a large difference is unlikely - The two groups have been shown to have the same mean weight - There is a 54% chance that the null hypothesis is really true - The study failed, so the result should not be reported ::: ## Score and take-home **Your score: ** ::: {.incremental} - The **outcome type**, the **number of groups** and **pairing** come from the design - **Describe** before you test: n (%), mean (SD) or median (IQR) - **Check** for impossible values; report what you excluded - Report **effect size + 95% CI + p**, in a sentence ::: **Next:** Session 2: checking assumptions

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
